watering: Every 7-10 days. Water when the top 2-3 inches of soil are dry.
soil: Chunky, well-draining aroid mix with perlite and bark
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and humans if eaten
description: The iconic Swiss cheese plant, famous for its glossy heart-shaped leaves that develop dramatic splits and holes as it matures. A fast, forgiving grower that makes a bold statement in any bright room.
careTips: Give it a moss pole or trellis to climb for larger, more fenestrated leaves.
Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth every few weeks to keep them glossy and dust-free.
Brown edges usually mean the air is too dry or watering is inconsistent.
Fertilize monthly in spring and summer with a balanced liquid feed.
Repot every 2 years into a pot one size larger.

watering: Every 2-3 weeks. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
sunlight: Low light to bright indirect light
soil: Gritty cactus or succulent mix with excellent drainage
toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs if chewed
description: An architectural, nearly indestructible plant with upright, sword-shaped leaves. It tolerates neglect, dim corners and irregular watering, which makes it a perfect first plant.
careTips: Overwatering is the number one killer. When in doubt, wait another week.
Reduce watering to once a month in winter.
Use a pot with drainage holes, ideally terracotta.
Rotate the pot occasionally so the leaves grow evenly.
Propagate by cutting a leaf into sections or by dividing the rhizome.

watering: Every 7-10 days. Water thoroughly when the top 2 inches of soil are dry.
sunlight: Bright, indirect light with a few hours of gentle morning sun
soil: Rich, well-draining potting mix with perlite
toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs if eaten
description: A statement tree with large, violin-shaped leaves and a sculptural form. Beautiful but particular: it likes consistency in light, water and location, and dislikes drafts and being moved.
careTips: Pick a bright spot and keep it there. Moving the plant often causes leaf drop.
Rotate a quarter turn each week so it grows straight rather than leaning.
Brown spots that spread from the center usually point to overwatering or root rot.
Keep it away from air conditioners, heaters and open doors.
Dust the large leaves regularly so they can photosynthesize efficiently.

watering: Every 5-7 days. Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy.
soil: Peat-based, moisture-retentive potting mix with good drainage
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and humans if eaten
description: A graceful plant with dark green leaves and elegant white blooms. It is also a dramatic communicator: the leaves droop clearly when thirsty and bounce back within hours of watering.
careTips: Water when the leaves just begin to droop, then drain the saucer.
Use filtered or rested tap water if the leaf tips turn brown.
Direct sun scorches the leaves; a bright north-facing window is ideal.
Few flowers usually means it needs more light.
Mist or group with other plants to raise the humidity.

watering: Every 7-10 days. Water when the top inch or two of soil is dry.
soil: All-purpose potting mix with added perlite
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and humans if eaten
description: A cheerful trailing vine with heart-shaped, variegated leaves. It thrives on neglect, grows quickly, and looks great in hanging baskets, on shelves or trained up a moss pole.
careTips: Yellow leaves usually mean too much water. Let the soil dry a little more.
Pinch back long vines to encourage fuller growth.
Variegation fades in low light, so give it brighter conditions to keep the patterns.
Propagate easily by rooting stem cuttings in water.
Fertilize lightly every 4-6 weeks during the growing season.

watering: Every 2-3 weeks. Allow the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
sunlight: Low light to bright indirect light
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and humans if eaten; may irritate skin
description: A tough, glossy plant with waxy, upright stems that stores water in thick underground rhizomes. It handles low light and long gaps between waterings better than almost any houseplant.
careTips: Never let it sit in water. Soft, yellowing stems signal overwatering.
Growth is slow, so avoid frequent repotting and heavy fertilizing.
Wipe the leaves occasionally to keep them shiny.
Wash your hands after handling because the sap can irritate skin.
It will tolerate dim offices and bedrooms, but grows faster with brighter light.

watering: Every 2-3 weeks. Soak thoroughly, then let the soil dry out completely.
sunlight: Bright light with some direct sun
soil: Sandy, gritty succulent mix in a pot with drainage holes
toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs if eaten
description: A spiky, sun-loving succulent whose thick leaves store a soothing gel traditionally used on minor burns. It is easy to grow on a sunny windowsill and produces plenty of baby plants.
careTips: Place it in the sunniest window you have. Leggy, flat growth means it needs more light.
Mushy or translucent leaves indicate overwatering.
Use terracotta pots to help the soil dry faster.
Separate the offsets (pups) once they have a few leaves to create new plants.
Water less in winter when growth slows.

watering: Every 7-10 days. Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry.
soil: Well-draining potting mix with perlite or bark
toxicity: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs; the milky sap can irritate skin
description: A bold houseplant with thick, glossy, deep green or burgundy leaves. More forgiving than its cousin the fiddle leaf fig, it grows into a striking indoor tree with minimal fuss.
careTips: Wipe the large leaves with a damp cloth to keep them glossy.
Dropping lower leaves can mean overwatering or too little light.
Prune the top to encourage branching and control height.
Turn the pot regularly so it grows evenly toward the light.
Wear gloves when pruning because the sap is irritating.

watering: Every 5-7 days. Keep the soil evenly moist but not waterlogged.
sunlight: Medium to bright indirect light, never direct sun
soil: Light, airy, peat-based mix that holds moisture and drains well
description: A showpiece with broad, round leaves striped in silver and green. The leaves fold up at night in a daily motion called nyctinasty, but the plant is sensitive to dry air, tap water and bright sun.
careTips: Use distilled, filtered or rainwater. Tap minerals cause crispy brown edges.
Keep humidity high with a humidifier or a pebble tray.
Curling leaves mean it is thirsty or the air is too dry.
Avoid direct sun, which fades and scorches the stripes.
Keep it away from cold drafts and heating vents.

watering: Every 7 days. Keep the soil lightly moist and let the top inch dry out.
description: A cheerful, arching plant with striped green and white leaves that sends out dangling baby plantlets. It is adaptable, pet-friendly and one of the easiest houseplants to propagate.
careTips: Brown tips are often caused by fluoride and chlorine in tap water or by dry air.
Pot up the plantlets in soil or root them in water to make new plants.
It likes being slightly root-bound, so repot only when roots crowd the pot.
Provide bright indirect light for the best variegation and more plantlets.
Feed lightly every month during spring and summer.
